sources.title: Yemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterway
sources.excerpt: Saudi-backed forces gave conflicting reports of whether they had also seized the port city of Mokha, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
sources.text: Yemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterway. Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement. The Yemeni military also said in a statement that its forces had captured the Red Sea city of Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes. But in conflicting reports, unnamed Yemeni government and military sources later told news agencies Reuters and AFP that the forces had only reached the city's outskirts. The Houthis denied losing Bab al-Mandab and Mokha and said they had struck Riyadh's airport and other locations in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the air strikes. Saudi Arabia condemned the attacks and reiterated calls for the UN Security Council's permanent members to support Yemen's internationally-recognised government. Turkey and Pakistan, allies of Saudi Arabia, meanwhile held an emergency meeting in Riyadh and agreed to rapidly deploy military forces to Saudi Arabia in an invocation of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, according to a statement shared by Pakistan's foreign ministry. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", in a statement to AFP. The offensive launched by the pro-government National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces in south-western Yemen on Monday reportedly saw the Houthis pushed out of most of the coastal areas they seized last month. Four government sources told Reuters that Yemeni forces had reached the outskirts of Mokha late on Monday, and that Houthi fighters were now retreating. Government military sources who spoke to AFP would not confirm the capture of the city, but said: "Our forces took control of the Dhubab military airfield and cut the road linking the Dhubab district to the Bab al-Mandab area." Earlier, the Yemeni military also said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town. Houthi‑run media cited a Houthi military source as rejecting as "Saudi propaganda" the claims that the group had lost control of Mokha, and that the group remained in control of Dhubab, Bab al‑Mandab and the Kahboub mountains near the coast. The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital, Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago. Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive. Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV. Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences". The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations". On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis. Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia". It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded. The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory. In addition to the strikes on Riyadh's international airport, the Houthis attacked an Aramco oil refinery, and Abha airport, as well as other sites, according to Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree in a statement on Telegram. According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east. A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island. They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia. However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. sources.title: Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war
sources.excerpt: The BBC's Frank Gardner speaks to some of those who have fled the war by crossing the Red Sea to Djibouti.
sources.text: Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war. Ibrahim Issa, 50, is from the Yemeni coastal town of Dhubab, right on the front lines of the war between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-backed pro-government forces fighting them. Today he sits, surrounded by his family, on a tarpaulin spread over a sandy floor inside a vast open-sided warehouse at Markazi camp in Obock, northern Djibouti, packed with Yemeni families who have fled by boat across the narrow Bab al-Mandab Strait. After their sea crossing, Yemeni refugees have made their way by truck and on foot to this camp, jointly administered by the government and the UN. "How could I just sit there when my kids are screaming and shaking in terror?" says Ibrahim Issa. "When the sound of the planes start, and the kids hear the planes, they begin shouting and screaming. As parents it is our responsibility, what can you do when you see this? That is why we fled, to save them." As a fisherman, Ibrahim Issa already owned a boat large enough to bring out his family from Yemen. He even brought several of the family's goats which I can now see nibbling at scraps nearby, foraging amidst the discarded canisters of cooking gas and empty plastic bottles. Some families have been able to bring small bundles of possessions with them from Yemen – one family has even brought a "jeraak", a tall metal shisha pipe – but others have arrived, exhausted, in just the clothes they left in. In just the last few days more than 3,000 refugees have arrived here from Yemen, many entire families. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast. This month, the country's Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen years ago, made a lightning dash down the coast towards Bab al-Mandab, the narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government of Yemen, has responded with hundreds of air strikes along the flat, coastal plain where the Houthis are now digging in. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia. "We don't care which side it is that's attacking," is the message I got loud and clear in Arabic from everyone here I spoke to. "It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee." Djibouti, a tiny former French colony that sits just across the water from Yemen, has made it clear it has no intention of involving itself in the war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. And yet Djibouti is one of the most militarised nations in Africa. Since 2003, the US has run a huge multinational base here, Camp Lemonnier, once home to the French Foreign Legion. China too has a major base here, its largest military presence on the Indian Ocean and recently upgraded. Back in Markazi camp, one of those I spoke to is Qassim Abraham Abssy. Once also a fisherman, his identity card shows him to be 100 years old. "It was the planes. The sounds of the planes, boom! That's what made us flee, for the sake of our children. It burns ours hearts. We don't know which side they are from. They are bombing everywhere, because the Houthis are everywhere, in the mountains, in the roads. A plane comes, bombs everywhere." Outside in the blazing 37C heat, close to the neat lines of tents supplied by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, I met Mohammed Abdullarim from Aden, a 63-year-old former tour guide old enough to have been born when Aden was still a British protectorate. Unlike the new arrivals, Mohammed has been here since 2015. He fled to Djibouti soon after the fighting first flared up between the Houthis and the government of the now-ousted President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi. He has been at the camp ever since but suddenly, as we were talking, the sadness of what is happening to his country overwhelmed him and he turned his head away, choking back tears. "Most of the people here are in the worst condition, inside the tents here. I am very touched, I'm crying for these people, for my people, for their suffering. I want our voices to be heard by the NGOs and the Djibouti government. And I'm thankful to them for accepting us." How long will they have to stay here? That depends, of course, on the fighting. Yemen has been wracked by a horrific civil war that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions since 2014. A shaky, UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis has broken down spectacularly in recent months, with the two sides trading missiles, drones and air strikes. Yemen's war may be a remote one to most people but the effect of choking off Saudi Arabia's oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab Strait are well publicised. But as ever, it is often the human cost that goes unnoticed. Sitting beside his wife on their tarpaulin, amid the cacophony all around them, Qassim Abssy the fisherman is wary of leaving the safety of Djibouti: "If the war continues then we're not going back because we have peace here." His wife, Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed, agrees. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country, and we are praying to God that peace does return. All we need is peace, even for our children's future, they get safety first, then food, water and an education. "As you see we just fled with our clothes, and left everything behind, because [in Yemen] there is no peace."

sources.title: [Freightos Weekly Update] Premier Alliance joins Red Sea return
sources.excerpt: Middle East crude exports are approaching pre-war levels via the Strait of Hormuz and alternatives according to some estimates, with prices easing moderately; bunker costs remain roughly flat for now ...
sources.text: [Freightos Weekly Update] Premier Alliance joins Red Sea return. 1. Middle East crude exports are approaching pre-war levels via the Strait of Hormuz and alternatives according to some estimates, with prices easing moderately; bunker costs remain roughly flat for now though, as increased crude volumes may take time to translate into lower refined product prices. 2. Saudi crude flows via the southern Red Sea are contributing to the recovery, with Saudi-backed forces attempting to recapture Houthi-seized positions on the Bab el-Mandeb; despite these ongoing tensions, the Premier Alliance – the last major holdout – has announced some services will resume Red Sea transits this month. 3. Asia-Europe rates slipped 2-3% last week to $3,260/FEU to N. Europe and $3,555/FEU to the Mediterranean, with Med prices back to pre-peak season levels even with Far East congestion still a factor. The sharper decline on Mediterranean lanes may reflect the sharper rebound in Red Sea transits compared to N. Europe lanes. 4. Transpacific rates eased 3% to $8,322/FEU on the West Coast while East Coast held at $9,600/FEU; Golden Week blanked sailings may help keep prices stable near term, and nearly three months of weather-related Far East port disruptions continue to absorb capacity and could keep the transpacific rate floor elevated even into the post-peak, pre-LNY demand lull. 5. Air cargo rates cooled over Golden Week, with Far East/China-N. America down more than 15% to $5.60/kg and Far East/China-Europe easing 7% to $3.83/kg/ • Asia-US West Coast prices (FBX01 Weekly) decreased 1% to $8,322/FEU. • Asia-US East Coast prices (FBX03 Weekly) stayed level at $9,606/FEU. • Asia-N. Europe prices (FBX11 Weekly) decreased 3% to $3,260/FEU. • Asia-Mediterranean prices (FBX13 Weekly) decreased 2% to $3,555/FEU. • China - N. America weekly prices decreased 18% to $5.60/kg. • N. Europe - N. America weekly prices increased 1% to $2.14/kg. Some recent estimations have Middle East crude oil exports – via the Strait of Hormuz and alternatives – approaching pre-war levels, with crude prices easing moderately. For now though, bunker prices remain about level with the last few weeks, as increased crude volumes, if sustained, may take time to translate into lower prices for refined products. Increased Saudi crude flows via the southern Red Sea account for part of this volume recovery, with Saudi-backed forces attempting to recapture areas on the Yemeni coast of the Bab el Mandeb Strait recently seized by the Houthis. Even with elevated tension in the region container carriers continue to gradually increase Red Sea traffic, with the Premier Alliance – the last holdout among the three alliances and MSC – announcing some services will resume Red Sea transits this month. The increase in effective capacity from more vessels taking the shorter route is likely one contributor to container rates sliding since mid-July on Asia - Europe lanes. Prices dipped 2-3% last week to $3,260/FEU to N. Europe and $3,555/FEU to the Mediterranean, with rates level so far this week over the Golden Week holiday as carriers have blanked sailings during this low demand stretch. The sharper increase in Red Sea sailings for Asia - Mediterranean services, as well as continued challenges with congestion at some N. Europe hubs for Asia - N. Europe volumes, may explain why rates to the Mediterranean – even as Far East congestion, though improving, continues to tie up capacity – have slid back to pre-peak season levels. Asia - N. Europe prices meanwhile, remain about $400/FEU higher than back in mid-May. Transpacific container rates decreased 3% to the West Coast last week to $8,322/FEU while East Coast prices were level at $9,600/FEU. Increased blanked sailing over the Golden Week period may help keep prices stable in the near term. Increases in blanked sailings as well as backlogs from nearly three months of weather-related disruptions at major ports in China may keep the transpacific rate floor quite elevated even as we enter what is normally a couple months of low demand post-peak season and pre-Lunar New Year rush. In air cargo, more recent analyses confirm data center components are a significant driver of global demand growth even as e-commerce volumes – though still significant – contract in some major markets. The Freightos Air Index shows Far East/China rates cooling more than 15% to N. America last week to $5.60/kg and easing 7% to Europe to $3.83/kg as demand eases over Golden Week.

sources.title: The New Red Sea Wars
sources.excerpt: For much of the past century, policymakers have treated the Horn of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula as separate strategic regions divided by the Red Sea. That distinction is now evaporating. Wars on ...
sources.text: The New Red Sea Wars. The spread of the conflict in Sudan is part of a larger geopolitical transformation. For much of the past century, policymakers have treated the Horn of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula as separate strategic regions divided by the Red Sea. That distinction is now evaporating. Wars on one side of the sea increasingly alter the military calculations on the other. This entanglement is only deepening in the wake of the United States’ and Israel’s decision in February to launch a war on Iran, driving a deeper wedge between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh (which were already at odds), weakening the American-anchored security order in the region, and underscoring the importance of securing the Red Sea for shipping. For the past decade, the UAE has been the most aggressive outside player in the Horn of Africa, establishing ports and military bases, offering large financial packages to key allies, and involving itself extensively in Sudan’s civil war. But the recent war in Iran, along with the breakdown of the Emirati-Saudi security partnership in Yemen last December, made Riyadh less confident of Washington’s protection, more anxious about the UAE’s security ties to Israel, and more intent on controlling the Red Sea’s security picture. And so as Saudi Arabia has leaned into an alignment with Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan, it has also brought that alignment to bear to strengthen key partnerships in the Horn. It is trying to counter factions in the Horn that are backed by the UAE or Israel even as it struggles to manage threats from Iran and its allies—including the Houthis, who have seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. At the same time, the risk of conflict is increasing between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), backed by Saudi Arabia and its allies, and Ethiopia, an ally of the emirates, as well as the chance that another direct war could erupt between Ethiopia and Eritrea. A new war between Ethiopia and Eritrea on the Red Sea would likely turn into a regional conflict that overlaps with the one in Sudan. And it would not only be aggravated by the existing Emirati-Saudi rift—it might well deepen that divide. Some Middle Eastern governments once saw the Horn of Africa as a low-stakes theater in which they could compete for leverage at relatively little cost. But as wars in the Middle East and the Horn become inextricably linked, a single security sphere is coalescing. Unless leaders in both the Middle East and the Horn recognize how interconnected their security dilemmas have become, instability will continue to ricochet in both directions, and the overlapping conflicts and disputes will become harder to resolve. In some respects, the growing entanglement between the Horn of Africa and the Middle East is a return to a historical norm. Over millennia, the sea connected present-day Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Yemen, and people, goods, and cultural trends moved regularly among them. Amharic, Ethiopia’s dominant language, and Tigrinya, widely spoken in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, are both Semitic tongues. Christianity spread early to what is now northern Ethiopia, making it home to one of the world’s oldest Christian Orthodox traditions. In the sixth century, an Aksumite ruler based in modern-day Ethiopia briefly conquered parts of Yemen. Not long afterward, the Prophet Muhammad sent some of his earliest followers across the Red Sea to take refuge with a Christian Aksumite king there. Islam later spread across the sea and along Africa’s Indian Ocean coast. From the sixteenth to the twentieth century, the Ottoman Empire ruled territory on both sides of the Red Sea, and Omani rulers built an empire tying the Arabian Peninsula to much of East Africa’s coastline, eventually moving their capital from Muscat to Zanzibar. These links persisted into the modern age. When the Saudi kingdom conquered the Hejaz region on the western Arabian Peninsula in the early twentieth century, elites in the port city of Jeddah sent their families across the Red Sea to Port Sudan for safety. And in April 2023, when war erupted in Khartoum, many Sudanese took refuge in Jeddah. Starting in the twentieth century, however, a separation began to harden between the two sides of the Red Sea as European colonialism and nationalist movements severed governance links crisscrossing the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Connections remained—for instance, Persian Gulf wealth flowed to nearby African countries and African labor and exports flowed the other way after a 1970s oil boom transformed the Gulf economies, and Middle East countries played a substantial role in a war during that decade between Ethiopia and Somalia. But the political gulf between the Arabian and African Red Sea shores widened further after the end of the Cold War. The first Gulf War, in 1990-91, upended the Middle East and expanded the U.S. military footprint there, giving Gulf states a reprieve from managing their near abroad. Around the same time, polities in the Horn began to fragment. Somalia’s collapse drove Somaliland, a former British colony along the Gulf of Aden, to claim independence in 1991. Regime change in Ethiopia led to the 1993 secession of Eritrea, and an intensified civil war in Sudan eventually prompted South Sudan’s 2011 secession. The United States made fraught and often counterproductive efforts to try to manage these convulsions in the Horn of Africa. Yet it rarely saw the Horn and the Middle East, or its role in each region, as linked. While Gulf states focused on threats emanating from Iran and the Levant, the Horn turned inward. Regional leaders in these areas also did not view them as intimately connected. East African leaders such as Ethiopian President Meles Zenawi primarily sought influence across the African continent rather than across the Red Sea, championing institutions such as the African Union. Influential Christian elites in both Ethiopia and Kenya, the Horn region’s two strongest countries, have little attachment to the Arab world.

sources.title: If the Red Sea Landscape Changes… Is Sudan Ready?
sources.excerpt: Rifai Abulhasan Tensions ease and intensify, but the Red Sea does not wait for anyone… So, has Sudan prepared its ports, coastline, ...
sources.text: If the Red Sea Landscape Changes… Is Sudan Ready?. Adel Al-Rifai Abulhasan Tensions ease and intensify, but the Red Sea does not wait for anyone… So, has Sudan prepared its ports, coastline, infrastructure, and maritime capabilities to receive ships and frigates and protect its interests when the landscape changes? Major events may take place far from Sudan, or close to it, without us having any hand in them or being a party to them. That does not, however, prevent their repercussions from reaching us. Tensions in the eastern Mediterranean ease and intensify from time to time. The region may appear calm at one moment, only for tensions to resurface and escalate, potentially signalling major developments at any time. Maritime routes are interconnected, and what happens in the eastern Mediterranean, the Strait of Hormuz, or the Bab el-Mandeb Strait can affect the Red Sea, shipping, trade and energy, as well as the security of Sudanese ports and coastline. The eastern Mediterranean matters to Sudan because of its links to trade routes and our exports and imports, particularly to Europe. As for the Strait of Hormuz, despite its importance, some of its routes may have alternatives. We should therefore view developments through the lens of Sudan’s interests, its geographical position, and the nature of its trade. This is where the Prudence Principle comes in: if a development could have a significant impact, preparing for it becomes a duty, even if we are not a party to it. A responsible state does not wait for a crisis to begin thinking; it prepares in advance. The relevant authorities must not merely monitor events, but turn monitoring into an operational system: information must be collected, analysed, and linked to the direction of events, while benefiting from cooperation and information-sharing with counterpart agencies in friendly countries. Developments in the eastern Mediterranean—in tensions, interests and alliances—should be viewed through a Sudanese lens: What do they mean for the Red Sea? What could they mean for our ports, our trade, and our security? The Sudanese coastline is not merely a maritime boundary; it is Sudan’s gateway to the world and its artery for foreign trade. Our exports pass through it, our imports enter through it, and it is connected to food and energy supplies and to the stability of the economy. Developing and protecting it is therefore simultaneously a security, economic and national issue. From here, the question can be turned into a clear action plan: First: Ports and Infrastructure Improve the efficiency of ports, berths, and maritime services, and ensure they can receive commercial and naval vessels in accordance with technical and legal requirements, while providing refuelling, provisioning, maintenance, and support services. Second: Monitoring and Early Warning Establish an integrated system to monitor the coastline and maritime traffic, based on radar, communications, tracking systems, and maritime information, linking relevant authorities through a shared operational picture. Third: Human and Maritime Capabilities Develop personnel, enhance training, and benefit from joint maritime exercises and drills with friendly countries to improve capabilities, transfer expertise, and familiarise personnel with the latest technologies. Fourth: Agreements and International Cooperation Review existing maritime agreements and understandings, identify which can be activated, and turn them into practical cooperation that serves the Sudanese Navy, ports, trade, and the economy. Fifth: Survey and Exploration Conduct a comprehensive marine survey using modern technologies to determine what lies beneath our waters and seabed in terms of resources, from minerals, raw materials and fisheries to the potential for oil and gas. Sixth: Protection of Resources and Facilities Establish a system to protect future maritime resources and facilities, covering production, transportation, and export, and address maritime, environmental, and operational risks from the discovery stage rather than after production begins. Seventh: Turning the Red Sea into an Opportunity-Generating Economy Ports and maritime and logistics services, exploration, mining, energy, fisheries and related industries should not be treated as separate files. Rather, they can form links in a single economic chain, beginning with resources and ending with projects, production, added value, employment opportunities and new expertise for the people of Sudan. The ongoing war in Sudan has taught us a lesson that must not be wasted. It has exposed strengths and weaknesses, and demonstrated the importance of training and capacity-building, electronic warfare, reconnaissance and tracking, autonomous and unmanned systems, and the rapid development of the tools of warfare. These lessons should therefore translate into a practical review of capabilities, needs, and priorities, rather than becoming mere memories of the war. This, in turn, opens the way to establishing an integrated national system for managing the Red Sea and the Sudanese coastline, bringing together all relevant authorities and operating under a unified vision while coordinating information, responsibilities, and priorities. In this way, the Red Sea would become a comprehensive national portfolio combining security, trade, investment, exploration, resource protection, port development and maritime capabilities. Such a system does not require waiting for ideal circumstances. It can begin with a comprehensive assessment of the current situation, followed by identifying gaps, setting priorities, and developing specific projects with timetables, clearly defined responsibilities, funding sources and measurable indicators. This would enable Sudan to move from talking about the Red Sea to acting on it. The objective is not simply to prepare for war, nor to wait for a potential crisis. It is to build a national capability that functions in peacetime, remains operational during crises, and protects Sudanese trade,

sources.title: Red Sea crisis
sources.excerpt: The Red Sea crisis is an ongoing armed conflict and maritime crisis instigated by the Houthis, an armed group in Yemen. The Houthis began launching missiles and armed drones at Israel in response to the Gaza war, and have seized or attacked dozens of merchant and naval vessels travelling through the Red Sea which they…
sources.text: Red Sea crisis. The Red Sea crisis is an ongoing armed conflict and maritime crisis instigated by the Houthis, an armed group in Yemen. The Houthis began launching missiles and armed drones at Israel in response to the Gaza war, and have seized or attacked dozens of merchant and naval vessels travelling through the Red Sea which they claimed are linked to Israel. These actions provoked a military response from Israel, as well as the United States and the United Kingdom. The crisis is linked to the Middle Eastern crisis, the Iran–Israel proxy conflict, and the Yemeni crisis.
